summary: Initial discovery focused on per-token unit economics and throughput/latency tradeoffs between Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployment modes. Customer emphasized tight 99th-pct latency SLO for transactional underwrites and strict budget cap per 1M requests. Redwood AE/SE explained batching, prefix/KV caching, quantization, and reserved capacity implications. Agreed next steps: cost spreadsheet, pilot runbook, and sample logs for benchmark.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private cost tradeoffs
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-20
Time: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~56 minutes
Attendees: Liam Parker (Redwood AE), Nadia Ortiz (Redwood SE), Erin Walsh (Product, ScoutTech), Rajiv Menon (CTO, ScoutTech), Dana Liu (ML Engineer, ScoutTech)

[00:00] Liam (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick intro, I'm Liam Parker, account exec at Redwood Inference, and with me is Nadia Ortiz, our solutions engineer. How are you all?
[00:08] Erin (ScoutTech): Hey Liam, thanks. Erin here. We'll try to keep this focused — goal for today is to understand raw unit cost implications for our underwriting flow and to see which deployment mode makes sense.
[00:16] Rajiv (CTO): Hi, Rajiv. I'm responsible for infra decisions. Short background: we have a transactional LLM call per underwriting decision, avg tokens 350 input + 150 output, percentiles are spiky, want p99 < 250ms ideally. Budget constraint: roughly $2k-$3k/month for the initial pilot; longer term we can expand if unit economics look good.
[00:36] Dana (ML): Dana, ML Eng. I'll probably run the pilot and provide logs. We use mostly 2-stage flow: prompt + small reranker for candidate selection.
[00:45] Nadia (Redwood SE): Great context. Just to align: use case is transactional inference where latency matters more than slightly cheaper per-token, correct?
[00:53] Rajiv: Correct, but we also can't blow the budget. So we're trying to find the sweet spot — minimize cost per decision while keeping p99 under the SLO.
[01:05] Liam: Perfect. Quick agenda: we'll walk through our hosted pricing simple model, then talk about Dedicated reserved capacity and Private (VPC/on-prem) high-level tradeoffs. Nadia will cover batching, caching, and quantization levers, and then we can map that to your traffic profile and budget.

[01:20] Erin: Sounds good. Could you start with hosted per-token costs? We saw some numbers in the quickstart but need realistic examples for 8k vs 32k context.
[01:29] Liam: Sure. For hosted, our list per-token is tiered by model family and context length. Rough example numbers we discussed offline — e.g., for an 8k context open model variant you'd pay X per input token + Y per output token — I'm going to give a worked example in the spreadsheet we'll send. Important caveat: the effective cost also depends on batching and cache hit-rate, which Nadia will explain.

[01:50] Nadia: Right — two levers that materially change per-decision cost: batching (combining concurrent requests into a single forward to amortize KV and attention cost) and prefix/KV caching (if much of your prompt is static). For transactional underwriting, do you have a large static prefix?
[02:03] Dana: Yes, about 60% of our prompt is static boilerplate: policy text, instructions. The dynamic part is applicant fields and variables.
[02:12] Nadia: That's good. With a 60% static prefix, prefix caching can reduce the per-call compute substantially — you basically only compute the dynamic suffix tokens on many requests if the cache hit is valid. Note: with short interactions, you may see diminishing returns at small batch sizes.

[02:29] Speaker 1: um, quick question — caching is session based or is it per-key?
[02:33] Nadia: Great question. We support prefix caching keyed by canonicalized prefix and by model version. It's TTL-based, and for Dedicated/Private customers you can pin cache policies and share across instances. Hosted isolates cache per-customer but still gives good hit rates when prompts are consistent.

[02:50] Rajiv: Regarding batching — our peak concurrency is about 60 qps during spikes, but average concurrency is 10. How does batching interact with p99 latency? We can't queue requests for long.
[03:04] Nadia: Continuous batching in our runtime aims to keep batching windows very tight — typical micro-batch wait is 5-10ms to collect concurrency. In practice, for your profile, we can tune the max batch size and the micro-batch wait to keep 99th percentile impact minimal. At 60 qps, batching helps a lot on cost. But yes, there's a small latency tax on some percentage of requests when waiting for a batch to form.

[03:24] Erin: Can you quantify the tradeoff? If we accept +20ms median and +60ms p99, what sort of unit-cost delta are we seeing? Ballpark numbers are fine.
[03:34] Liam: Ballpark: if you're at single-request execution (no batching) cost per decision might be ~1.0x baseline. With effective batching at your concurrency and good cache hits, you can get to ~0.6x or even 0.45x per-call cost depending on model size and quantization. Exact numbers depend on tokens per call and batch occupancy. We'll produce a table showing these scenarios.

[03:58] Dana: Quantization — is that something we can use for hosted? Our risk team is picky about determinism and output quality.
[04:06] Nadia: Hosted supports multiple precision/quantization-backed model variants. Quantized weights change numerical noise and sometimes minor token-level differences, but for many classification/rerank tasks they are fine. For underwriting we should validate on your prompts. Dedicated and Private let you pick more aggressive quantization if you want to squeeze cost.

[04:26] Rajiv: Walk me through how Dedicated pricing would compare. We have a predictable steady-state of 15 qps outside spikes.
[04:34] Liam: Dedicated is a reserved capacity model — you commit to certain GPU pool size and get predictable throughput and lower per-token compute price because you amortize the hardware. For a sustained 15 qps workload, Dedicated can be 30-60% cheaper per token than Hosted depending on the commit level and model. The tradeoff: you pay for reserved capacity month-to-month whether you use it fully or not. For pilot budgets under $3k/month, Hosted might be lower upfront cost.

[04:58] Erin: And Private on-prem? Probably out of scope for this pilot but we want to understand long term.
[05:03] Liam: Private is the option when data residency, air-gapped, or strict compliance is required. Costs are more operational: license/platform fee + infra. For large enterprise SLA and long-term volume it can be the cheapest per-token, but requires more ops ownership. We'll include a TCO sketch comparing 12/24 month horizons.

[05:21] Speaker 2: There's also network egress and data transfer business — is that material?
[05:25] Nadia: For typical text workloads it's minor compared to compute, but if you're doing high-volume embeddings or sending large context chunks it can show up. We'll call it out in the spreadsheet.

[05:37] Rajiv: Ok. A concrete ask: with our sample of 100k decisions/month, each ~500 tokens total, what's the expected monthly cost in Hosted vs Dedicated with caching assumptions? Could you give a ballpark?
[05:50] Liam: Off the cuff — Hosted with no caching and conservative batching: assume 500 tokens * 100k = 50M tokens. At a sample rate of $0.00002 per token (example, varies by model), that's $1k for the month — but that number is sensitive. With realistic batching and 60% prefix caching you might only actually compute ~40% of tokens on average, dropping to $400-$600. Dedicated could be cheaper for that volume but requires a monthly commit maybe starting at $3k-$4k depending on GPU choices. We'll enumerate break-even points.

[06:20] Dana: That hosted per-token example seems low compared to other vendors we've looked at. Are there hidden costs?
[06:27] Nadia: Sometimes customers forget to include inference pre/post-processing cost, orchestrator overhead, or embedding costs if used. Also, if you choose a larger model or require 32k context, per-token cost increases. We'll show model-variant examples.

[06:40] Erin: We might run a small reranker on top of generation — how should we think about multi-step flows?
[06:47] Nadia: Two ways: chain calls (generation -> rerank) or use a single multi-output call with structured output. Chain calls multiply compute stepwise. If reranker is small you can run a lightweight vector-based rerank (embeddings + cosine) which shifts cost profile to more embedding compute (cheaper per vector for many providers) but increases storage/cost for nearest-neighbor ops. We'll help model both flow costs.

[07:10] Speaker 1: You mentioned fallback policies earlier — if Dedicated saturates, what's the real behavior?
[07:14] Liam: We have smart routing: you can define fallback to Hosted or a smaller model variant. For production-critical flows we recommend a two-tier approach: Dedicated primary, Hosted fallback. There are configuration knobs for graceful degradation: reduce max tokens, lower model size, or reroute to cached answers.

[07:33] Rajiv: For pilot, we need to keep costs under the $3k cap. Which path do you recommend?
[07:38] Liam: For pilot under tight budget, Hosted with a well-designed cache and batching plan is lowest risk and lowest upfront cost. We can run a short benchmark to estimate real-world savings and then see if Dedicated makes sense as you scale.

[07:49] Erin: Ok, let's talk about the benchmark. What do you need from us?
[07:53] Nadia: Ideally: 1) 2 weeks of anonymized request traces (timestamps, input token counts, static prefix frequency), 2) 5-10 representative prompt templates, and 3) expected concurrency profile. With those, we can run a Redwood-hosted benchmark and return a detailed cost per-decision matrix.

[08:12] Dana: We can share logs but need to scrub PII. Is there a template?
[08:16] Liam: Yes, we'll send a log scrub template and a secure upload link. Also we'll include the SOC2 and security pack for hosted.

[08:24] Erin: Regarding performance, you said micro-batch windows are about 5-10ms. Our SRE will freak out if p99 goes above 250ms. How do you measure p99 and attribute to batching vs model compute?
[08:36] Nadia: Our telemetry breaks down token compute time, kernel latency, and queueing/batching wait. We'll instrument the same metrics in the pilot. You can set SLO alerts in the Console for model-level p99. If batching pushes requests over the SLO, we can adjust the max wait to prioritize latency.

[08:52] Rajiv: Any examples of customers who did similar transactional workloads? We want references for latency-sensitive deployments.
[08:58] Liam: We have a couple in fintech who needed p99 < 300ms. One used Dedicated with small-model quantization for core path and Hosted fallback during peaks. We can share anonymized case notes.

[09:10] Erin: Pricing transparency is critical internally. Will you share a per-token calc and show sensitivity to cache hit rate and batching occupancy?
[09:17] Liam: Absolutely. We'll build a sensitivity table: axes will be cache hit-rate (0-80%), average batch occupancy, and model variant. That'll show break-even across Hosted vs Dedicated.

[09:28] Speaker 3: A little side note — are there ways to artificially reduce tokens per prompt? Rewriting prompts or more structured inputs?
[09:33] Dana: We already use dense fields but could explore structured extraction. That might help a lot.

[09:37] Nadia: Yes, prompt engineering and template compression are low-effort wins. Another trick is to move static data to the cache and only provide a canonical key in the prompt. Also consider hybrid rerank — a small retrieval index reduces generation length. We'll add these recommendations to the runbook.

[09:55] Erin: Can you explain how reserved capacity billing works? If we commit to a pool, can we scale down during a month?
[10:02] Liam: Commit is monthly with autoscale policies. You can autoscale down but reserved minimum affects pricing tiers. There's also burst capacity options to cover short spikes beyond reserve. We'll detail the economics for partial month utilization in the spreadsheet.

[10:16] Rajiv: For SLA — what uptime/latency guarantees do you provide for Dedicated vs Hosted?
[10:21] Liam: Dedicated comes with an SLA for uptime and a latency objective per model family; Hosted has strong coverage but enterprise-grade latency SLOs are part of Dedicated/Private contracts. We'll include the SLA excerpts.

[10:33] Erin: Any gotchas with switching model versions during rollouts? We want to pin model versions for experiments.
[10:38] Nadia: You can pin versions and do canary rollouts. There is some warmup time for cache/KV and KV cache invalidation semantics if you change prompt templates. We'll plan rollouts carefully in the pilot runbook.

[10:51] Dana: If we do private on-prem later, can we reuse the same prompts and traffic profile from Hosted? Migration friction?
[10:58] Liam: Yes — the API and abstractions are the same. Biggest friction is operator setup and quantization parity. We work with your infra team to reproduce runtime kernel selections to match behavior.

[11:10] Erin: This is helpful. Quick question on embeddings — not core to the pilot but we may use them for retrieval. How does embedding cost compare?
[11:18] Nadia: Embeddings are billed separately — typically cheaper per call but you pay for vector storage and nearest-neighbor ops. If you swap generation for retrieval+rerank, cost profile can improve.

[11:29] Rajiv: Okay final operational question: for the pilot, how do we control costs if something goes wrong?
[11:33] Liam: You can set per-key quotas, rate limits, and route unknown traffic to lower-cost model variants. We'll help set conservative caps for the first two weeks.

[11:44] Erin: Great. Let's recap and next steps. Liam?
[11:47] Liam: Recap: 1) ScoutTech will provide scrubbed request logs and prompt templates, 2) Redwood sends cost/throughput spreadsheet and benchmark plan, 3) schedule a 2-hour pilot planning session, 4) run a 1-week hosted benchmark with defined SLOs. Action items listed in the doc.

[11:58] Rajiv: Sounds good. Anything else?
[12:00] Dana: One tiny ask — can you include a worst-case cost estimate if caching fails (0% hit rate)? We want to plan for that scenario.
[12:07] Nadia: Yep; sensitivity table will include 0% case.

[12:11] Erin: Ok, thanks everyone. We'll coordinate internally and expect your doc.
[12:15] Liam: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and runbook.
[12:20] (Call ends)

Notes: transcription contains occasional mis-hearings for tech terms (e.g., "K V cash" instead of "KV cache") consistent with auto-transcript artifacts. References: shared drive link to "ScoutTech-redwood-benchmark.xlsx" (sic), SOC2 summary link, pilot runbook draft (to be uploaded).
